Time Complexity Basics

➢O(n²)       -   Quadratic

Time Complexity Basics

O(1) – Constant Time
•  The number of steps stays the same, no matter how
   big the input is.
•  Opening a box with a key. Whether the box has 1
   item or 1,000 items, it’s just one turn of the key.
•  Accessing an array element by index → always one
   step.

Time Complexity Basics

O(n) – Linear Time
•  Steps grow directly with input size.
•  Checking every student’s name in a class list. If there
   are 10 students, 10 checks. If 100 students, 100
   checks.
•  Linear search → look through each item until you find
   the target.

Time Complexity Basics

O(log n) – Logarithmic Time
•  Steps grow slowly, because the problem shrinks by
   half each time.
•  Looking up a name in a phone book by opening in the
   middle, then halving again.
•  1,000,000 names → only about 20 steps!
•  Binary search, balanced trees.
•  Logs = “counting how many times you can cut the
   pile in half.”

Time Complexity Basics

O(n²) – Quadratic Time
•  Steps grow as the square of input size.
•  Comparing every student with every other student in
  a class.
      •  10 students → 100 comparisons.
      •  100 students → 10,000 comparisons.
•  Bubble sort, nested loops

LIFO

LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) is a method used in data
structures and inventory accounting where the last item
added is the first one removed.
• Common in stack-based operations (e.g., undo
  features, browser history)
• Opposite of FIFO (First-In, First-Out)

LIFO

Imagine a stack of plates in a cafeteria:
• You add clean plates to the top of the stack.
• When someone needs a plate, they take the one
  from the top.
• The last plate added is the first one taken

LIFO

Used in stack data structures, where operations follow
this order:
•   Push → Add item to the top
•   Pop → Remove item from the top

LIFO

In accounting, LIFO assumes:
•   The most recent inventory is sold first.
•   Older inventory remains on the books.

Useful during inflation to reduce taxable income (higher
cost of goods sold).

STACKS

The stack data structure has three main methods:
•  push() method adds a node to the top of the stack
•  pop() method removes a node from the top of the stack
•  peek() method returns the value of the top node without
  removing it from the stack.

STACKS

•  Every stack has a size that determines
  how many nodes it can accommodate
•  Attempting to push a node in a full stack
   will result in a stack overflow
• program may crash due to a stack

STACKS

Stack is a data structure that follows
•  last in, first out (LIFO) protocol.
• The latest node added to a stack is the node which is
   eligible to be removed first.
•  If three nodes (a, b and, c) are added to a stack in
   this exact same order, the node c must be removed
   first.
• The only way to remove or return the value of the
  node a is by removing the nodes c and b.

Dijkstra’s algorithm: initialize and select
1. Set the source distance to 0 and all others to ∞. Start with no visited vertices and no predecessors.

4. Mark u visited. Its shortest distance is final.

Dijkstra’s algorithm: repeat
5. Keep selecting the nearest unvisited vertex and relaxing outgoing edges. Stop when all vertices have been visited or the remaining vertices are unreachable.

Bellman–Ford algorithm: origins
The algorithm is named for Richard Bellman and Lester Ford Jr., who contributed to shortest-path and network algorithms.

BELLMAN–FORD ALGORITHM
Bellman-Ford computes shortest paths from
a single source in weighted graphs that may
include negative edge weights, and it can
detect negative-weight cycles reachable from
the source

Bellman–Ford algorithm: goal and edge types
Find minimum-cost paths from one source, or detect a reachable negative-weight cycle. Directed edges can have negative weight. An undirected edge can be represented as two opposing directed edges, so a reachable negative undirected edge creates a negative cycle.

Bellman–Ford algorithm: output and complexity
Return distances and predecessors or report a reachable negative-weight cycle. Relax every edge up to V − 1 times and check once more for an improvement. Worst-case time is O(VE).

Bellman–Ford algorithm: initialization
Set dist[s] = 0 for source s and dist[v] = ∞ for each other vertex. Every predecessor starts unset.

Bellman–Ford algorithm: relax edges
For each directed edge u → v of weight w(u, v), check whether u is reachable and dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v]. If so, update dist[v] and set pred[v] = u. Repeat for up to V − 1 passes.

Bellman–Ford algorithm: detect negative cycles
After the relaxation passes, look for an edge u → v with finite dist[u] and dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v]. Such an improvement indicates a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source.

Bellman–Ford algorithm: why V − 1 passes?
A simple path visits each vertex at most once and therefore has at most V − 1 edges. When shortest distances are finite, a shortest path can be chosen to be simple. Further improvement after V − 1 passes indicates a reachable negative cycle.

MST
A spanning tree of a graph is a subset of edges that connects all
vertices together without forming any cycles.
• A minimum spanning tree (MST) is a spanning tree with the
minimum possible total edge weight

Minimum spanning tree: properties
Spans every vertex of the graph. A spanning tree has V − 1 edges and no cycles. An MST has the least total weight among all spanning trees. Distinct edge weights guarantee a unique MST.

MST
USE
Network design: Build cost-efficient road, telecom, or electrical
networks
Clustering in machine learning: MST helps group data points by
minimum linkage
Approximation algorithms: Used in solving complex optimization
problems (e.g., traveling salesman)

KRUSKAL'S ALGORITHM
a greedy method used to find the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of
a connected, weighted, undirected graph
works by repeatedly adding the smallest edge that doesn't form a
cycle until all vertices are connected
• Builds the MST by sorting edges by weight and adding them one by
one, ensuring no cycles are formed

KRUSKAL'S ALGORITHM
Step-by-Step Process
1. Sort all edges in non-decreasing order of weight.
2. Initialize MST as empty.
3. Iterate through edges:
a) Pick the smallest edge.
b) If adding it does not form a cycle, include it in the MST.
c) If it forms a cycle, discard it.
4. Repeat until MST has (V-1) edges (where (V) is the number of
vertices).
5. Cycle detection: Usually done with the Union-Find (Disjoint Set
Union) data structure.

PRIM'S ALGORITHM
greedy algorithm for finding a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)
of a connected, weighted, undirected graph
• Unlike Kruskal's (which is edge-based), Prim's grows the
MST vertex by vertex
• Starts from a chosen vertex and repeatedly adds the
cheapest edge that connects the tree to a new vertex

Prim’s algorithm: steps
1. Choose any starting vertex.
2. Find a lowest-weight edge connecting the current tree to an outside vertex.
3. Add that edge and its new endpoint.
4. Repeat until the tree includes all V vertices and has V − 1 edges.

Prim and Kruskal: how the tree grows
Prim grows one tree outward from a starting vertex. An array-based implementation works well for dense graphs. Kruskal examines edges in weight order and merges components, making it convenient for sparse edge lists. Both find an MST of the same total weight when given the same graph.
